# The foreman command

<!-- Generated by `npm run docs:cli` from the command table. Do not edit by hand. -->

The `foreman` command drives the running Foreman app from a terminal: start workspaces from templates, send and wait for turns, change settings, manage repositories, pull requests, schedules and remote workspaces. It talks to the app over a local socket in the data folder (a named pipe on Windows) that only you can read, so Foreman must be running. Install it from **Settings → Advanced → foreman command → Install**, or from a checkout with `npm run build && npm link`.

`foreman help` lists everything:

```text
foreman · drives the running Foreman app

Work           run, wait, send, cancel, resume-at, checks, status, report, review, ask, new,
               approvals, approve, deny, stopped
Workspaces     export, import, ws (21 commands: foreman help ws)
Chats          tabs, tab new|set|close|reopen|fork, chat, queue, rewind, resume-now, mcp, slash,
               search
Git & PRs      git (18 commands: foreman help git), diff, commits, comments, base-moved, ack-ci
Repositories   repos, repo (22 commands: foreman help repo)
Settings       templates, settings, env, keys, github, gitlab, loadouts, review-model, models,
               agents, commands, schedules, connections,
               slack rules|people|deliveries|answer|resend, linear issues, backup, git-backup
Remote         cloud (12 commands: foreman help cloud)
App            app info, doctor, cli status|install, completion, help, data, usage, attention

foreman help <command>   options, examples and exit codes       foreman help exit-codes | agents | settings-keys | environment
Every command takes --json. Inside an agent turn, foreman report and foreman review are the commands to know.
foreman --version prints the command’s version and the running app’s.
```

## Exit codes

```text
Exit codes, the same for every command:

  0  Done (wait: the turn completed; checks: they passed)
  1  Failed; or the turn failed, was stopped or was interrupted; or a check failed
  2  Usage error (unknown command or option, a bad value); or wait timed out; or checks errored
  3  Setup held (run); or checks are not configured
  4  Busy (checks while an agent turn is active)
  5  Foreman isn't running, or the connection to it dropped
  6  Needs confirmation or consent (--yes is missing, or what you were shown has changed)
  7  Refused by policy (a turn token on a command that changes setup, or agents may not start work)
  8  Not found or ambiguous (workspace, repository, tab, template…)

wait's 2 and checks' 2 and 3 overlap with usage errors by history; their own help says which is
which, and the JSON they print says it in words. A command that fails with --json also writes one
JSON object to stderr: {"error": "…", "code": "not-found"}, where code is one of not-running,
unknown-method, invalid, not-found, ambiguous, refused, busy, needs-confirmation, needs-consent,
not-supported or failed.

Earlier versions of foreman gave 1 for every failure. Any non-zero code is still a failure.
```

## Inside an agent turn

```text
Agents and the foreman command

Inside an agent turn Foreman sets FOREMAN_SESSION_ID, FOREMAN_TURN_ID and FOREMAN_TURN_TOKEN. Every
foreman command run there carries them, so a report lands on that tab and turn. The token is
attribution, not a security boundary: an agent can leave it out, and the app says so when a call
comes without one.

What an agent may call
  foreman report needs-input|stuck|checkpoint|done "<text>"   tell the user how the work is going
  foreman review "<what to check>"                            ask for a review (a row on Home)
  foreman checks                                              run the repository's configured checks
  foreman status, templates, repos, wait, cancel              read and manage turns (a turn can't wait for itself)
  foreman run, send, resume-at                                only with the repository's opt-in (below)

Starting work needs the user's say-so: Repository settings → Actions → "Let agents start workspaces and queue messages"
must be on for the repository the agent works in.

What an agent may not do
  Anything that changes how Foreman is set up or moves data out of it (export, import, cli install, and
  settings as they arrive) is refused with exit code 7: "Settings can't be changed from inside an agent turn."

Repository settings → Actions → "Teach agents Foreman" adds these instructions to the agent's own.
```

## Environment variables

```text
Environment variables the foreman command reads

  FOREMAN_DATA_DIR      The app's data folder (where cli.sock and cli.token live). Default: the app's own folder.
  FOREMAN_PASSPHRASE    The passphrase for export and import, so a script needn't type it.
  FOREMAN_SESSION_ID    Set by Foreman inside an agent turn: the chat the call comes from.
  FOREMAN_TURN_ID       Set by Foreman inside an agent turn: the turn.
  FOREMAN_TURN_TOKEN    Set by Foreman inside an agent turn: proves the two above. Don't set it yourself.
  FOREMAN_JSON=1        Same as --json on every command.
  NO_COLOR              Respected; the output is plain text already.
```

## Work

### foreman run

```text
Start a workspace with a filled-in template

Usage:
  foreman run <template> [value...] [options]

Arguments:
  <template>              A template’s slug, name, id or any unique part of it (`foreman templates` lists them)
  <value...>              Values for the template’s {{placeholders}}, in order (optional)

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>  Repository to start the workspace in (default: the one you’re in)
  -b, --branch <name>     Name for the new branch (default: named from the prompt)
      --base <branch>     Branch to start from (default: the repository’s base branch)
  -l, --loadout <n>       Agent and model from loadout slot n (default: 1)
  -o, --open              Bring Foreman forward on the new workspace
  -n, --dry-run           Print the filled-in prompt; create nothing
      --start-anyway      If setup fails, send the first message anyway
      --no-wait           Return once the workspace exists, without waiting for setup
      --wait              Block until the first turn ends, and report how it went
      --timeout <s>       With --wait (and for `wait`): stop waiting after s seconds
      --with <a,b>        Integrations to switch on in this workspace (linear, slack), over the repository’s defaults
      --without <a,b>     Integrations to switch off in this workspace

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman run fix-a-bug "ENG-123: login button does nothing" --open
  foreman run issue https://github.com/owner/repo/issues/12
  foreman run fix-linear-bug ENG-123 --wait --timeout 1800
  foreman run triage ENG-123 --with linear --without slack

Exit codes:
  0  Started (with --wait: the turn completed)
  1  Failed, or the turn failed, was stopped or was interrupted
  2  Usage error, or --wait timed out (the turn keeps running)
  3  Setup failed; the first message is held
  5  The connection to Foreman was lost (the turn is unaffected)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Values fill the template's {{placeholders}} in order; extra values join the last one.
A GitHub issue or PR URL as a value also attaches its text as a file; a PR URL checks out
its head (fetched from the repository the URL names) with the PR's base branch as the base.
An issue URL fills {{issue id}}.
The repository is the one you're in, unless --repo says otherwise.

If setup fails, the first message is held, not sent. The command prints the end of
the setup log and exits with code 3; use --start-anyway to send it regardless.

foreman run prints the workspace, chat (session) and turn ids. With --wait it then blocks
for that turn's outcome; `foreman wait <turn>` does the same later, also after the turn
has ended, because the outcome is read from the chat's saved record. Exit codes: 0 completed,
1 failed, stopped or interrupted, 2 timed out (the turn keeps running), 3 setup held,
5 the connection to Foreman was lost (the turn is unaffected). --json adds the outcome,
what the turn changed, the checks state and the pull request URL. The Foreman app must be
running for any of this: the turn runs in the app, and so does the waiting.
```

### foreman wait

```text
Wait for a turn’s outcome

Usage:
  foreman wait <turn> [--timeout s] [--words] [--json]

Arguments:
  <turn>             The turn id that `foreman run` and `foreman send` print

Options:
      --timeout <s>  Stop waiting after s seconds; the turn keeps running
      --words        One sentence, for a screen reader: “Claude Code finished in api-fix: this turn 3 files, +120 -14. Checks: 12 passed.”

Common options:
      --json         Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet        Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes          Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help         Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman wait 7f3a9c --timeout 600
  foreman wait 7f3a9c --words
  foreman wait 7f3a9c --json

Exit codes:
  0  Completed
  1  Failed, stopped or interrupted
  2  Timed out (the turn keeps running)
  5  The connection to Foreman was lost (the turn is unaffected)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

The outcome is read from the chat’s saved record, so waiting after the turn finished still answers. --words prints the outcome as the narrator’s sentence (this turn’s change, or the workspace’s when the turn has none, labelled; checks as recorded, “stale” when the files have changed since); with --json it changes nothing. The Foreman app must be running.
```

### foreman send

```text
Queue a message into a chat tab

Usage:
  foreman send <workspace> [--tab n] <template|text...>

Arguments:
  <workspace>         A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in
  <template|text...>  A template’s name, id or slug followed by its values, or the words of a message

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>       Open tab to send to, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)

Common options:
      --json          Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet         Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes           Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help          Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman send api "Also add a test for the empty case"
  foreman send . --tab 2 fix-a-bug "flaky login test"

foreman send queues a message into one tab of a workspace (a name, id or branch from
`foreman status`, or "." for the one you're in). The first word may be a template's exact
name, id or slug, followed by its values; otherwise everything after the workspace is the
message (put -- before text that starts with a dash). A workspace with one open tab needs
no --tab; with several, send refuses and lists the tabs (index, title, model, status). It
never steers a running turn. It prints the receipt: "Queued to tab 2 (Claude · Opus 5.5)
as turn <id>". An idle tab starts the turn at once ("Sent to tab ...").
```

### foreman cancel

```text
Cancel a queued, starting or running turn

Usage:
  foreman cancel <turn> [--json]

Arguments:
  <turn>       The turn id that `foreman run` and `foreman send` print

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman cancel 7f3a9c

foreman cancel takes the turn id that foreman run and foreman send print: a queued turn
is dropped, a starting or running one is stopped, and it prints the outcome.
```

### foreman resume-at

```text
Arm the “Resume at …” a usage-limit failure offers (or disarm it)

Usage:
  foreman resume-at <turn> [--cancel] [--json]

Arguments:
  <turn>        The turn that hit the usage limit

Options:
      --cancel  Disarm the resume instead

Common options:
      --json    Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet   Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes     Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help    Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman resume-at 7f3a9c
  foreman resume-at 7f3a9c --cancel

Arming ticks the same “Resume at …” box on the usage-limit card in the chat; the chat then continues by itself once the limit resets.
```

### foreman checks

```text
Run this workspace’s configured checks

Usage:
  foreman checks [--json]

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman checks
  foreman checks --json

Exit codes:
  0  Passed
  1  Failed
  2  Error, timeout or cancelled
  3  Not configured
  4  Busy: an agent turn is active in the workspace
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

foreman checks runs the commands under [[checks]] in the workspace you're in, with the
same definitions and records as the Git panel's Run checks. Exit codes: 0 passed,
1 failed, 2 error, timeout or cancelled, 3 not configured, 4 busy (an agent turn is
active in the workspace; try again when it ends).
```

### foreman status

```text
List workspaces and what each needs

Usage:
  foreman status [--words] [--json]

Options:
      --words  A line saying how many things need you, then a sentence per workspace, instead of the table

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman status
  foreman status --words
  foreman status --json

foreman status is read-only. It lists each workspace with its state (the same groups as
the sidebar), its latest turn, the state of its checks (passed, failed, stale, running,
incomplete or none), what that turn changed, and its pull request. --words prints a line saying how many things need
you, then one sentence per workspace (“api-fix: Claude Code finished 2 minutes ago, this turn 3 files +120 -14, checks
12 passed, PR #51 open.”), for a screen reader; with --json it changes nothing. Every command needs the Foreman app to
be running.
```

### foreman report

```text
Tell Foreman, as the agent, how the work is going

Usage:
  foreman report needs-input|stuck|checkpoint|done "<text>" [--link url]

Arguments:
  <kind>            What kind of report (one of: needs-input, stuck, checkpoint, done)
  <text...>         A few words saying it (optional)

Options:
      --link <url>  A link to show with the report

Common options:
      --json        Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet       Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes         Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help        Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman report needs-input "Which database should the migration target?"
  foreman report done "Fixed the login redirect" --link https://github.com/owner/repo/pull/12

foreman report and foreman review are for agents. Inside an agent turn Foreman sets
FOREMAN_SESSION_ID, FOREMAN_TURN_ID and FOREMAN_TURN_TOKEN, so a report lands on that tab and
turn; without them it counts for the workspace you're in, and says so. needs-input and stuck
stay on Home as "agent says" until the user replies in that tab or dismisses them; checkpoint
and done are quiet lines in the chat. The token is attribution, not a security boundary.
A call carrying a turn token can't use run or send unless the repository allows it
(Repository settings → Actions → "Let agents start workspaces and queue messages").
```

### foreman review

```text
Ask the user for a review (adds a row on Home; starts nothing)

Usage:
  foreman review "<what to check>"

Arguments:
  <what...>         What the user should look at

Options:
      --link <url>  A link to show with the request

Common options:
      --json        Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet       Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes         Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help        Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman review "The migration in db/20261024_add_index.sql"

foreman review adds a row on Home asking the user to look at something; it starts nothing.
Like foreman report it is for agents: see `foreman help report` and `foreman help agents`.
```

### foreman ask

```text
Ask Foreman about your workspaces and get a spoken-style answer

Usage:
  foreman ask "<question>" [--workspace ws] [--json]

Arguments:
  <question...>                What you want to know, in your own words

Options:
      --workspace <name|id|.>  The workspace you mean (a name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in) (default: none: the assistant looks across all of them)

Common options:
      --json                   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet                  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman ask "what needs me?"
  foreman ask "did the checks pass?" --workspace .
  foreman ask "which workspaces are idle?" --json

Exit codes:
  0  Answered
  2  Timed out (what it had so far is printed)
  3  The assistant isn’t available: off, Privacy mode or no signed-in agent
  7  Called from inside an agent turn
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

foreman ask runs one turn of the Foreman assistant (the Ask Foreman overlay) with its read-only state
tools, waits for it and prints the answer in plain sentences. --workspace gives it the workspace you mean (a name, id
or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you're in); without it the assistant looks across all of them.
If the assistant proposes a command, ask prints it as a line you can run yourself: "Proposed: <what it does>" and
"Run it yourself: foreman <words>". It never runs the proposal, and the proposal is dropped from the Assistant view, so
nothing waits there. The question leaves no conversation in the Assistant view either. It gives up after two minutes
and prints what it has (exit 2). With --json it prints {answer, proposals: [{runId, command, summary}], timedOut?}.

It needs the assistant: it is refused under Privacy mode, when the assistant is turned off in Settings, and when no
agent is signed in, with the reason on stderr and exit code 3. It is an admin command, so it is never served to an
agent from inside a turn (exit 7), and the assistant itself can't propose it, because it runs the assistant.
Exit codes: 0 answered, 2 timed out, 3 the assistant isn't available, 7 called from an agent turn.
The Foreman app must be running.
```

### foreman new

```text
Start a workspace from a prompt, without a template

Usage:
  foreman new <prompt...> [options]

Arguments:
  <prompt...>              What to work on, in your own words (quote it, or put -- before text that starts with a dash)

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>   Repository to start the workspace in (default: the one you’re in)
  -b, --branch <name>      Name for the new branch (default: named from the prompt)
      --existing <branch>  Check out this existing branch in a new worktree
      --direct <branch>    Work in the repository folder itself, on this branch
      --base <branch>      Branch to start from (default: the repository’s base branch)
  -l, --loadout <n>        Agent and model from loadout slot n (default: 1)
      --attach <file>      A file for the first message (repeatable)
      --cloud              Put the worktree in a cloud sandbox
  -o, --open               Bring Foreman forward on the new workspace
      --start-anyway       If setup fails, send the first message anyway
      --no-wait            Return once the workspace exists, without waiting for setup
      --wait               Block until the first turn ends, and report how it went
      --timeout <s>        With --wait: stop waiting after s seconds
      --with <a,b>         Integrations to switch on in this workspace (linear, slack), over the repository’s defaults
      --without <a,b>      Integrations to switch off in this workspace

Common options:
      --json               Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet              Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help               Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman new "Add a dark mode toggle to the settings page" --open
  foreman new "Why did the eval scores drop?" --with linear
  foreman new "Fix the flaky login test" -b fix-flaky-login --wait --timeout 1800
  foreman new "Review this" --existing feature/search --attach notes.md

Exit codes:
  0  Started (with --wait: the turn completed)
  1  Failed, or the turn failed, was stopped or was interrupted
  2  Usage error, or --wait timed out (the turn keeps running)
  3  Setup failed; the first message is held
  5  The connection to Foreman was lost (the turn is unaffected)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

foreman new starts a workspace from the words you give it, with no template, the way the New
workspace dialog does. The repository is the one you're in unless --repo says otherwise; the
agent and model come from loadout slot 1 unless -l picks another. By default the branch is
new and named from the prompt: -b names it, --existing checks out a branch that already
exists in a new worktree, and --direct works in the repository folder on that branch. --attach
copies files into the first message (relative paths are taken from where you run it). --cloud
puts the worktree in a cloud sandbox (the repository's Remote settings apply).

Like foreman run, it waits for setup and prints the workspace, chat and turn ids; with --wait
it then blocks for the first turn's outcome, with the same exit codes as foreman run
(0 completed, 1 failed, 2 timed out, 3 setup held, 5 connection lost). From inside an agent
turn it needs the repository's "Let agents start workspaces and queue messages".
```

### foreman approvals

```text
List what agents are waiting on

Usage:
  foreman approvals [list]

Arguments:
  <list>       Optional; listing is all this does (one of: list) (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman approvals
  foreman approvals --json

One row per request: id, workspace, tab, kind (tool, plan or question) and the ask. Answer with foreman approve or foreman deny.
```

### foreman approve

```text
Approve a tool, plan or question an agent is waiting on

Usage:
  foreman approve <id> [--always|--edits] [--message "…"] [--plan] [--feedback "…"] [--answer "question=choice"]...

Arguments:
  <id>                            The request’s id from `foreman approvals` (or the start of it)

Options:
      --always                    Tool: allow it from now on, when the tool offers that
      --edits                     Tool: allow edits for the rest of the session, when offered
      --message <text>            Tool: a note to the agent with the answer
      --plan                      Plan: approve it (checked against the request’s kind)
      --feedback <text>           Plan: a note with the approval
      --answer <question=choice>  Question: one answer per question (repeatable)

Common options:
      --json                      Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet                     Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                       Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                      Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman approve 3f9a
  foreman approve 3f9a --always
  foreman approve 5c21 --plan --feedback "Skip step 4"
  foreman approve 8d07 --answer "Which database?=Postgres"

foreman approvals lists what agents are waiting on: a tool asking permission, a plan to review
or a question. approve and deny answer one by its id (or the start of it, four characters or
more). For a tool, --always or --edits give the "allow from now on" and "allow edits for the
session" answers, when that tool offers them. For a plan, --feedback adds a note, and deny sends
the plan back with --message as the feedback. For a question, give --answer "question=choice"
once per question (the question's text, header or position from 1); deny skips it.

Answering lets an agent act, so approve and deny are refused from inside an agent turn.
```

### foreman deny

```text
Deny a tool, send a plan back or skip a question

Usage:
  foreman deny <id> [--message "…"]

Arguments:
  <id>                  The request’s id from `foreman approvals` (or the start of it)

Options:
      --message <text>  Tell the agent why (a tool’s reason, a plan’s feedback)

Common options:
      --json            Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet           Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes             Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help            Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman deny 3f9a --message "Use the staging database"
  foreman deny 5c21 --message "Split it into two PRs"

foreman approvals lists what agents are waiting on: a tool asking permission, a plan to review
or a question. approve and deny answer one by its id (or the start of it, four characters or
more). For a tool, --always or --edits give the "allow from now on" and "allow edits for the
session" answers, when that tool offers them. For a plan, --feedback adds a note, and deny sends
the plan back with --message as the feedback. For a question, give --answer "question=choice"
once per question (the question's text, header or position from 1); deny skips it.

Answering lets an agent act, so approve and deny are refused from inside an agent turn.
```

### foreman stopped

```text
Review turns a quit or crash stopped

Usage:
  foreman stopped [list|retry|dismiss] [key] [--all]

Arguments:
  <verb>       What to do (list when left out) (one of: list, retry, dismiss) (optional)
  <key>        retry, dismiss: a turn id (or the start of it) or checks:<workspace id> (optional)

Options:
      --all    dismiss: clear every entry

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman stopped
  foreman stopped retry 7f3a9c
  foreman stopped dismiss --all --yes

When Foreman quits or crashes with turns running, they are listed here until you retry or
dismiss each. retry sends the turn's message again in its tab (it starts a turn, so from inside
an agent turn it needs the repository's "Let agents start workspaces and queue messages").
dismiss clears an entry without sending anything; --all clears every entry.
```

### foreman checks approve

```text
Approve the check commands a workspace would run, and run them

Usage:
  foreman checks approve [<workspace>] [--yes]

Arguments:
  <workspace>  A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman checks approve
  foreman checks approve api --yes

Exit codes:
  6  Not confirmed (no --yes and no terminal, or you answered no), or the commands changed since you read them
  8  No checks are configured
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Lists each command with its hash and whether it is approved, asks, then approves exactly the commands shown and starts the checks. If a command changes meanwhile nothing is approved.
```

## Workspaces

### foreman export

```text
Write a .foreman file: an encrypted backup, or chats you reviewed

Usage:
  foreman export <workspace> [--out file] [--share]

Arguments:
  <workspace>           A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
      --out <file>      Where to write it (default: <workspace>.foreman in the current folder)
      --share           Write the chats you pick in the clear, for someone else, instead of an encrypted backup
      --chat <n|id>     With --share: a chat to include (repeatable) (default: every open tab)
      --tool-output     With --share: include tool output
      --no-attachments  Leave attached files out
      --bundle          Include the branch and uncommitted work (backups include it unless --no-bundle)
      --no-bundle       Leave the branch and uncommitted work out of a backup

Common options:
      --json            Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet           Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes             Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help            Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman export api --out api-backup.foreman
  foreman export api --share --chat 1 --out chat.foreman

foreman export writes a .foreman file of one workspace: its chats (the latest version of each
message), attached files by hash, review comments and the names (never the values) of its
variables. By default it is a backup, encrypted with a passphrase (asked for twice, or set
FOREMAN_PASSPHRASE). --share instead writes the chats you pick in the clear, for someone
else: --chat <n|id> (repeatable; default every open tab), --tool-output, --no-attachments, --bundle (branch + uncommitted work; backups include it unless --no-bundle).
It lists what the file holds so you can review it first.
```

### foreman import

```text
Stage a .foreman file and create a history-only workspace

Usage:
  foreman import <file> [--repo name] [--copy]

Arguments:
  <file>                  A .foreman file

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>  The repository to put the workspace in (default: the single suggestion, with --yes)
      --copy              Import it again as a copy, with new ids

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman import api-backup.foreman --repo api
  foreman import api-backup.foreman --yes

foreman import checks the file
(version, hashes, size limits, no path traversal or links) in a quarantine folder where
nothing runs, then creates a history-only workspace: the chats are readable and there is no
worktree. Foreman suggests a repository by remote URL and root commit; name it with --repo,
or accept a single suggestion with --yes. Importing the same export again needs --copy,
which mints new ids. Activate the workspace in the app once its branch exists locally.
```

### foreman workspace archive

```text
Archive a workspace (shows what it will do first)

Usage:
  foreman workspace archive <workspace> [--delete-branch] [--stop] [--yes]

Arguments:
  <workspace>          A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
      --delete-branch  Also delete the workspace’s branch
      --stop           Stop running tabs first instead of refusing
      --anyway         Carry on past a failed checkpoint or archive script

Common options:
      --json           Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet          Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes            Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help           Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman ws archive api
  foreman ws archive api --delete-branch --stop --yes

Exit codes:
  0  Archived
  1  A step failed and nothing was deleted, or you answered no
  6  Needs confirmation: run in a terminal or add --yes
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

foreman workspace archive first asks the app what archiving would do and prints it: the folder that
is removed (or stays, for a workspace added from disk or working in the repository folder),
tabs still running, uncommitted files (saved as a checkpoint first), commits not on the
remote, open terminals, Docker containers it would remove and the archive script. Then it
asks before doing it; --yes answers for you, and without a terminal and without --yes it
prints the preview and exits with code 6, having done nothing.

Archiving refuses while a tab is running unless --stop is given. --delete-branch also deletes
the branch. A failed checkpoint or archive script stops the archive before anything is deleted
(exit 1, with the step); --anyway carries on regardless. Progress is printed to stderr as each
step finishes. Unarchive brings the workspace back; forget deletes an archived one for good.
```

```text

workspaces in the repository start with, the account it acts as, and roughly what its tool definitions cost
(a turn carries them only while it is on). --on and --off apply from the next message; the chat's receipt
says so. Only a working connection that agents may use can be switched on: switching grants nothing the
connection doesn't allow. From inside an agent turn, switching one on needs the repository's opt-in
(Repository settings → Actions → "Let agents start workspaces and queue messages").
```

### foreman tab new

```text
  <workspace>           A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:

      --effort <level>  Effort level, when the model has one
```

### foreman tab set

```text
Change a tab’s title, agent, model or modes

Usage:
  foreman tab set <workspace> [--tab n] [--title t] [--agent a] [--model m] [--effort e] [--fast|--no-fast] [--plan|--no-plan] [--auto-accept-edits|--no-auto-accept-edits] [--include-note|--no-include-note]

Arguments:
  <workspace>                 A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>               Open tab, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)
      --title <title>         A new title
      --agent <agent>         Switch the agent (not while a turn runs)
      --model <model>         The model’s id or name
      --effort <level>        Effort level
      --fast                  Turn fast mode on
      --no-fast               Turn fast mode off
      --plan                  Turn plan mode on
      --no-plan               Turn plan mode off
      --auto-accept-edits     Claude: accept file edits without asking
      --no-auto-accept-edits  Claude: ask before file edits again
      --include-note          Send the workspace note with this tab’s messages
      --no-include-note       Stop sending the workspace note with this tab’s messages

Common options:
      --json                  Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet                 Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                   Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                  Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman tab set api --tab 2 --title "Migration"
  foreman tab set api --model opus --effort high
  foreman tab set api --plan

foreman tab set changes the tab's own settings, the same ones the composer's pickers change.
--agent switches the agent for that tab (with its default model unless --model says one) and
refuses while a turn is running. --model and --effort are checked against what the agent
lists. --plan, --auto-accept-edits and their --no- forms change what the agent may do without
asking, so they can't be used from inside an agent turn.
```

### foreman chat

```text

  foreman chat <workspace> [--tab n] [--tail n] [--since turn] [--tool-output]

Arguments:
  <workspace>         A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>       Open tab, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)
      --tail <n>      Only the last n turns

  foreman chat api --since 7f3a9c --json

foreman chat prints a tab's conversation as text: who said what, each tool call on one line
(with --tool-output, its output too), notices, and how each turn ended. Each message shows its
turn id, which foreman tab fork --turn, foreman rewind --turn and --since take. --tail n keeps
the last n turns; --since <turn> keeps what came after that turn. With --json the items are the
chat's own records (no thinking; tool output only with --tool-output).
```

### foreman queue

```text
See and change a tab’s queued messages

Usage:
  foreman queue <workspace> [--tab n] [list|remove <msg>|steer <msg>|move <msg> up|down|edit <msg> "text"]

Arguments:
  <workspace>    A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in
  <verb>         What to do (list when left out) (one of: list, remove, steer, move, edit) (optional)
  <message>      The queued message: its position from 1, or its id (optional)
  <text...>      move: up or down; edit: the new text (optional)

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>  Open tab, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)

Common options:
      --json     Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet    Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes      Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help     Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman queue api
  foreman queue api --tab 2 remove 1
  foreman queue api move 2 up
  foreman queue api edit 1 "Also cover the empty case"

The queue is the messages waiting behind a running turn. A message is named by its position
from 1 or its id (from `list`). move up sends it sooner. edit and move are checked against the
queue as it is when you run the command: when the queue changed meanwhile, or the message
already started, nothing changes and the command says so. steer delivers a queued message into
the running turn instead of waiting for it to end.
```

### foreman rewind

```text
Restore a tab’s files and conversation to before a turn

Usage:
  foreman rewind <workspace> [--tab n] --turn <id> [--yes]

Arguments:
  <workspace>        A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>      Open tab, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)
      --turn <turn>  Rewind to just before this turn (from `foreman chat`)

Common options:
      --json         Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet        Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes          Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help         Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman rewind api --tab 1 --turn 7f3a9c

Exit codes:
  0  Rewound
  1  You answered no
  6  Needs confirmation: run in a terminal or add --yes
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

foreman rewind restores the tab to just before a turn: the files go back to the checkpoint
saved then and the conversation continues from there. Work done after that turn is lost, so
it asks first (--yes answers for you). Find the turn id with foreman chat.
```


```text

  6  Needs confirmation: nothing was reverted

foreman git revert puts each named file back as it was where the branch started (the base branch), the same
as the Changes panel's Revert: uncommitted and committed changes to it are discarded, and a file the branch added
is deleted. Paths are from the workspace's root. It prints what it would do and asks first; --yes answers for you,
and without a terminal and without --yes it prints that and exits with code 6, having done nothing.
```

### foreman diff

```text
Print a workspace’s diff

Usage:
  foreman diff <workspace> [--scope source] [--stat] [--files] [--words]

Arguments:
  <workspace>           A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
      --scope <source>  Which changes: uncommitted, branch, staged, last-commit, last-3, pr, commit:<sha>, picked:<sha>,<sha> or turn:<id> (default: branch)
      --stat            One line per file with its additions and deletions
      --files           Only the names of the changed files, one per line
      --words           Sentences instead of the patch: each file, then each hunk with the lines added and removed

Common options:
      --json            Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet           Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes             Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help            Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman diff api
  foreman diff api --words
  foreman diff api --scope uncommitted --stat
  foreman diff api --scope commit:3f9a1c2 --files
  foreman diff api --scope turn:7f3a9c --stat

foreman diff prints the Changes panel's diff as unified text. --scope picks the source: uncommitted, branch, staged, last-commit, last-3, pr, commit:<sha>, picked:<sha>,<sha> or turn:<id>.
The default, branch, is everything since the branch left its base, uncommitted work included. --stat prints a line per
file with its additions and deletions, --files only the names (one per line, for scripts). A turn is kept as counts per
file, so turn:<id> prints counts only. --words prints sentences for a screen reader instead: a lead ("3 files changed,
+120 -14"), a line per file ("src/api.ts, modified, 12 added, 3 removed") and a line per hunk ("src/api.ts, hunk 2 of 4,
lines 40 to 58, near: handleLogin(: added: ...; removed: ..."); "near" is the text git puts after the hunk's @@, which may
not be a function. Nothing is changed.
```

### foreman comments

```text
List, add, edit, resolve or delete comments on a workspace’s diff

Usage:
  foreman comments <workspace> [list|add <file> <line> "<text>"|edit <id> "<text>"|resolve <id>|delete <id>]

Arguments:
  <workspace>  A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in
  <verb...>    list (the default), add <file> <line> <text>, edit <id> <text>, resolve <id> or delete <id> (one of: list, add, edit, resolve, delete) (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman comments api
  foreman comments api add src/login.ts 42 "Handle the empty password here"
  foreman comments api resolve 3f9a1c2d

Comments are notes on lines of the diff. Yours wait and go with the next message you send in any of the
workspace's chats, as the Changes panel's do (nothing is sent now); an agent's are open until resolved. `list` is the
default. `add` needs a file with changes in the diff (its path from the workspace's root), a line number and the text.
`edit` changes the text of a comment of yours that hasn't been sent. `resolve` marks one resolved; `delete` removes it.
A comment is named by its id from `list`, or the first four or more characters of it.
```

### foreman git pr auto-fix

```text
Turn auto-fix CI on or off for a workspace’s pull request

Usage:
  foreman git pr auto-fix <workspace> [--tab n] [status|on|off] [--yes]

Arguments:
  <workspace>    A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in
  <verb>         status (the default), on or off (one of: status, on, off) (optional)

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>  The tab the fixes are sent to (for `on`) (default: the only open tab)

Common options:
      --json     Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet    Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes      Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help     Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman pr auto-fix api status
  foreman pr auto-fix api on --tab 1
  foreman pr auto-fix api on --tab 1 --yes
  foreman pr auto-fix api off

Exit codes:
  0  Done
  1  Not changed (answered no)
  6  Needs confirmation: nothing was changed
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Auto-fix CI lets Foreman answer a failing CI run on its own: it sends the Fix errors message with the failure logs to one tab,
with no one asking, within a small budget per commit and per pull request. That is a consent, so `on` first prints what the
window's dialog shows (the tab and its agent, what that tab may do without asking, the exact instructions it sends and the budget)
and asks (--yes answers for you; without a terminal and without --yes it exits with code 6, having changed nothing). If the tab,
its permissions or the instructions change between the preview and the answer, Foreman refuses and you look again.
`status` says whether it is on and why it stopped; `off` turns it off. It can't be used from inside an agent turn.
```

### foreman repo settings

```text
Read and change a repository’s settings (the Repository settings window)

Usage:
  foreman repo settings [list|get|set|unset|file]

Arguments:
  <verb>       What to do; without one, this help (one of: list, get, set, unset, file) (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman repo settings
  foreman repo settings list --repo api

Repository settings have layers: this computer's value (local), the committed .foreman/settings.toml
(shared), your own Settings (user) and the default. `get` and `list` say which layer a value comes from;
`set` writes this computer's layer and says when it hides a shared value; `unset` removes it so the value is
inherited again. Keys are <tab>.<id> after the Repository settings tab: git.base-branch,
scripts.checks-after-turn, actions.prompt-general, repo.icon, integrations.github-account, cloud.vcpus.
Lists and text values take the forms `set` documents. The repository is the one you are in unless --repo says
otherwise.
```

### foreman repo settings set

```text
Change repository settings on this computer

Usage:
  foreman repo settings set <key> <value> [<key> <value>...] [--repo <name|path>]  |  <key> --add|--remove <item> | --stdin | --file <path>

Arguments:
  <key value...>          Pairs: a key, then its value

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>  Repository: a name, id or folder (default: the one you’re in)
      --add <item>        List settings: add an item to the current list (repeatable)
      --remove <item>     List settings: take an item out of the current list (repeatable)
      --stdin             Read the value from standard input: one item per line for a list, the whole text for a text setting
      --file <path>       Read the value from a file (an image file for repo.icon)

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman repo settings set scripts.checks-after-turn on --repo foreman
  foreman repo settings set actions.prompt-general --file prompt.md
  foreman repo settings set git.sensitive-paths --add secrets/ --add .env
  foreman repo settings set repo.icon emoji:🚀

Exit codes:
  2  A value is not valid for its key (nothing is written unless every pair is valid)
  7  Called from inside an agent turn
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Writes this computer's layer (updateRepoSettings), or the repository's own record for keys like repo.name and
cloud.vcpus. When a key is also set by the committed .foreman/settings.toml the answer says it overrides it.
Lists take a,b,c to replace them or --add / --remove to change them by an item. Text settings
(actions.prompt-*, cloud.install-script) take --file <path> or --stdin; the file is read here and its text sent.
repo.icon takes emoji:<emoji>, lucide:<name>, or --file with an image.
```

### foreman repo setup

```text
The steps that set up a new workspace

Usage:
  foreman repo setup [list | add <name> <command> | remove <name|n> | move <n> <m> | clear | inherit] [--repo <name|path>]

Arguments:
  <verb>                  list (the default), add, remove, move, clear or inherit (one of: list, add, remove, move, clear, inherit) (optional)
  <words...>              add: the name then the command; remove: a name or number; move: two positions (optional)

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>  Repository: a name, id or folder (default: the one you’re in)
      --timeout <s>       add: seconds before the step is stopped
      --parallel          add: run alongside the steps next to it
      --at <n>            add: position to insert at, from 1 (default: the end)

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman repo setup
  foreman repo setup add install "npm ci" --timeout 600
  foreman repo setup move 3 1
  foreman repo setup inherit --yes

Exit codes:
  6  clear or inherit without --yes and without a terminal to ask on
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Steps run in order when a workspace is created. Editing starts from this computer’s steps; with none, the committed ones are copied here first. `clear` empties the list; `inherit` drops this computer’s steps so the committed (or default) ones apply again. `list` is read-only and works from an agent turn.
```

```text
      --save    With --detect: link the repository to the account found

Common options:
      --json    Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet   Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes     Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help    Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman repo account
  foreman repo account api --detect
  foreman repo account api --detect --save

Without --detect, repo account says which GitHub account the repository uses. --detect asks `gh` which signed-in accounts can
push to the repository's remote and reports the only one that can; --save then links the repository to it (or clears a
link Foreman picked itself).
```

```text
Preview which ignored files a new workspace would get a copy of

Options:

  -h, --help            Show this command’s help

Nothing is copied or saved: it lists what the patterns would match among the repository’s gitignored files. Save patterns with `foreman repo settings set files-to-copy`.
```

## Settings

### foreman templates

```text
List templates and their {{placeholders}}

Usage:
  foreman templates [--json]

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman templates
  foreman templates --json

Lists your personal templates and, when you are in a repository, the ones in its .foreman/templates folder (marked "from repo").
```

### foreman settings

```text
Read and change Foreman’s settings (the Settings window, from a terminal)

Usage:
  foreman settings [list|get|set|reset|keys|search|path|export|import]

Arguments:
  <verb>       What to do; without one, this help (one of: list, get, set, reset, keys, search, path, export, import) (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman settings
  foreman settings list --changed
  foreman settings set appearance.theme dark

Keys are <page>.<id>, the page Settings shows the row on and the row's id: appearance.theme,
git.branch-prefix, cloud.max-running. `foreman settings keys` lists them; `foreman help settings-keys`
prints the table with what each takes. Booleans accept on/off (also true/false, yes/no, 1/0). Changes go
through the same service as the Settings window, so what the window does (apply now, a note about what
changed) happens here too. Settings can't be changed from inside an agent turn.
```

### foreman settings list

```text
Every setting with its value, grouped as Settings is

Usage:
  foreman settings list [--page <page>] [--changed] [--json]

Options:
      --page <page>  Only this Settings page (one of: general, account, appearance, accessibility, models, agents, git, environment, experimental, advanced, data, devices, cloud)
      --changed      Only the settings that differ from their default

Common options:
      --json         Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet        Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes          Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help         Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman settings list
  foreman settings list --page appearance
  foreman settings list --changed --json

A * marks a value that differs from the default. Inside an agent turn only the settings the assistant may read are listed.
```

### foreman settings get

```text
Show settings: value, default, where it is in Settings, what it takes

Usage:
  foreman settings get <key>... [--json]

Arguments:
  <key...>     One or more settings keys, like appearance.theme

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman settings get appearance.theme
  foreman settings get git.branch-prefix-type git.branch-prefix --json

Exit codes:
  2  A key is not a setting (the error names the nearest keys)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes
```

### foreman settings set

```text
Change one or several settings

Usage:
  foreman settings set <key> <value> [<key> <value>...]  |  foreman settings set <key> --add <item> | --remove <item> | --stdin

Arguments:
  <key value...>       Pairs: a key, then its value (quote values with spaces)

Options:
      --add <item>     List settings: add an item to the current list (repeatable)
      --remove <item>  List settings: take an item out of the current list (repeatable)
      --stdin          Read the value from standard input: one item per line for a list, the whole text otherwise

Common options:
      --json           Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet          Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes            Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help           Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman settings set appearance.theme dark
  foreman settings set git.branch-prefix-type custom git.branch-prefix yatin/
  foreman settings set environment.env-files --add .env.local
  git ls-files "*.env" | foreman settings set environment.env-files --stdin

Exit codes:
  2  A value is not valid for its key (nothing is written unless every pair is valid)
  7  Called from inside an agent turn
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Every pair is checked before anything is written. A list takes a,b,c to replace it, or --add / --remove to
change it by an item (the current list is read first). Each change prints "key value (was old)", plus a note
where the setting widens what an agent may do or deletes something.
```

### foreman settings reset

```text
Put settings back to their defaults

Usage:
  foreman settings reset <key>... | --all [--yes]

Arguments:
  <key...>     The settings to reset (optional)

Options:
      --all    Every setting; asks first (--yes skips the question)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman settings reset appearance.theme
  foreman settings reset --all --yes

Exit codes:
  6  --all without --yes and without a terminal to ask on
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Each key goes through the same owner as `set`, so a reset has the same side effects as choosing the default in Settings.
```

### foreman env set

```text
Save an environment variable

Usage:
  foreman env set <KEY> [VALUE] [--repo <name|path>] [--stdin]

Arguments:
  <KEY>                   Variable name
  <VALUE>                 The value. Without it: --stdin, or a prompt that does not echo (optional)

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>  Repository: a name, id or folder (default: the one you’re in)
      --stdin             Read the value from standard input (one trailing newline is dropped); it is never echoed

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman env set API_URL https://example.test
  printf %s "$TOKEN" | foreman env set MY_TOKEN --stdin
  foreman env set DATABASE_URL --repo api

Exit codes:
  2  No value given and no terminal to prompt on (use --stdin)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

A value on the command line lands in your shell history and in the process list; prefer the prompt or --stdin for anything secret.
The value is read from standard input or a prompt that does not echo it; it is never printed, logged or put on the command line by this command.
```

```text
Without --stdin, --from-shell or --remove the key is asked for at a prompt that does not echo. The value is read from standard input or a prompt that does not echo it; it is never printed, logged or put on the command line by this command.
```

### foreman templates add

```text
Save a new template

Arguments:

Options:

A template is a prompt with optional {{placeholders}} that `foreman run <template> <values…>` fills in order.
Its start model (--agent and --model) is what a new workspace opens with; a follow-up is the button offered when
a turn ends. Templates a repository keeps in .foreman/templates are read-only here: change the file instead.
Changing a template's text pauses the schedules that run it until you approve them again.
```

### foreman schedules preview

```text
Show what a schedule would approve and when it would run, without saving

Usage:
  foreman schedules preview <template> --every cadence --at HH:MM [--repo r] [--on days] [--day-of-month n] [--tz zone] [--start date] [--base b] [--model m] [--max-minutes n]

Arguments:
  <template>                A template’s slug, name or id; it must have no {{placeholders}}

Options:
  -r, --repo <name|path>    The repository each run works in (default: the one you’re in)
      --every <cadence>     once, hourly, daily, weekly or monthly (one of: once, hourly, daily, weekly, monthly)
      --on <days>           Weekly: the days, comma separated: mon,wed or weekdays (0 is Sunday) (default: the start date’s weekday)
      --day-of-month <n>    Monthly: the day, 1 to 31 (the last day in shorter months) (default: the start date’s day)
      --at <HH:MM>          Time of day, 24 hour, in the time zone
      --tz <zone>           An IANA zone, like Europe/London (default: this computer’s)
      --start <YYYY-MM-DD>  The first date it may run, in the zone (default: today there)
      --base <branch>       The branch each run starts from (default: the repository’s base branch)
      --model <id>          A Claude model id (default: a Sonnet from the picker)
      --max-minutes <n>     Stop a run after n minutes, 5 to 480 (default: 30)

Common options:
      --json                Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet               Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                 Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman schedules preview nightly-triage --repo api --every daily --at 09:00

A schedule starts a workspace from a template in a repository at a time. Saving it approves what it will run: the
template's text, the repository's setup script, its checks and its MCP servers. add and edit print that (the
fingerprint block below) and save only after you answer yes in a terminal or pass --yes; what you confirm is exactly
what is saved, and the app refuses if the setup, checks or template changed meanwhile. A change to any of them later
pauses the schedule until `foreman schedules approve <id>`. Runs happen only while Foreman is open; a late run is
skipped, never replayed; two failed runs in a row pause the schedule.

A scheduled run can't ask for values, so the template must have no {{placeholders}}: `foreman templates edit` writes
them out. `schedules add` takes no values for that reason.

What add, edit and approve print before they save anything (the fingerprint block):

  Schedule “nightly-triage” (template revision 3fa91c2)
  Repository: api, each run starts from main in a fresh workspace
  Runs every day at 09:00 (Europe/London), from 2026-10-26
  Next: Mon 26 Oct 09:00; Tue 27 Oct 09:00; Wed 28 Oct 09:00
  Runs on: Claude · claude-sonnet-5, permission mode auto; a question or an approval stops the run and leaves it for you
  Limit: 30 minutes per run
  Setup script: npm ci
  Checks: lint (npm run lint), test (npm test)
  Repository MCP servers: (none)
```

```text
Arguments:

Options:

Examples:
  foreman schedules add nightly-triage --repo api --every daily --at 09:00 --tz Europe/London
  foreman schedules add weekly-deps --repo api --every weekly --on mon,thu --at 08:30 --yes
  foreman schedules add release-notes --repo api --every monthly --day-of-month 1 --at 10:00

Exit codes:
  1  You answered no, so nothing changed
  6  Needs confirmation: run it in a terminal or add --yes
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

A schedule starts a workspace from a template in a repository at a time. Saving it approves what it will run: the
template's text, the repository's setup script, its checks and its MCP servers. add and edit print that (the
fingerprint block below) and save only after you answer yes in a terminal or pass --yes; what you confirm is exactly
what is saved, and the app refuses if the setup, checks or template changed meanwhile. A change to any of them later
pauses the schedule until `foreman schedules approve <id>`. Runs happen only while Foreman is open; a late run is
skipped, never replayed; two failed runs in a row pause the schedule.

A scheduled run can't ask for values, so the template must have no {{placeholders}}: `foreman templates edit` writes
them out. `schedules add` takes no values for that reason.

What add, edit and approve print before they save anything (the fingerprint block):

  Next: Mon 26 Oct 09:00; Tue 27 Oct 09:00; Wed 28 Oct 09:00
  Runs on: Claude · claude-sonnet-5, permission mode auto; a question or an approval stops the run and leaves it for you
  Limit: 30 minutes per run
  Setup script: npm ci
  Checks: lint (npm run lint), test (npm test)
  Repository MCP servers: (none)
```

### foreman connections add

```text
Connect an account

Usage:
  foreman connections add github|linear|slack|vercel|e2b|daytona|docker [--label name] [--token-stdin] [--default] […]

Arguments:
  <service>                   The service to connect (one of: github, linear, slack, vercel, e2b, daytona, docker)

Options:
      --label <name>          What to call it (default: the account’s name)
      --token-stdin           Read the token from standard input (without it a terminal gets a prompt that does not echo)
      --gh-account <login>    github: sign in as this `gh` account
      --gh-active             github: sign in as whichever `gh` account is active now
      --team-id <id>          vercel: the team id (team_…)
      --project-id <id>       vercel: the project id (prj_…)
      --domain <domain>       e2b: a self-hosted domain
      --api-url <url>         daytona: the API URL
      --target <region>       daytona: the target region
      --context <name>        docker: a Docker context
      --host <url>            docker: a host, like ssh://user@host
      --agent-access <level>  linear: what agents may do with it (one of: off, read, write) (default: read)
      --default               Make it the service’s default connection
      --allow-duplicate       Add it although a connection to the same account exists

Common options:
      --json                  Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet                 Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                   Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                  Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman connections add github --gh-account octocat --label Work
  printf %s "$LINEAR_API_KEY" | foreman connections add linear --token-stdin --label Acme
  foreman connections add vercel --team-id team_123 --project-id prj_456 --token-stdin
  foreman connections add docker --context colima

A connection is an account Foreman signs in to: GitHub, Linear, Slack, or a sandbox service for remote workspaces
(Vercel, E2B, Daytona, Docker). Secrets are never arguments: a token comes from standard input (--token-stdin) or
from a prompt that does not echo it, and never comes back in any output (at most its last four characters).

  github   --gh-account <login> (a `gh` account), --gh-active (whichever is active now), or a token
  linear   a Linear API key
  slack    a bot token (xoxb-…)
  vercel   a token, --team-id and --project-id
  e2b      an API key; --domain for a self-hosted domain
  daytona  an API key; --api-url (default https://app.daytona.io/api), --target
  docker   no token: --context or --host, or the current context
```

### foreman slack rules

```text
List, add, remove or consent to Slack notification rules

Usage:
  foreman slack rules [list|add|remove <id>|consent <id>] [--event e --recipient me|reviewer|channel …]

Arguments:
  <verb>                      list (the default), add, remove or consent (one of: list, add, remove, consent) (optional)
  <id>                        remove and consent: the rule’s id (or the start of it) (optional)

Options:
      --connection <id|name>  add: the Slack connection (default: the default Slack connection)
      --event <event>         add: what happens (one of: review-requested, pr-ready, ci-failed, changes-requested, pr-approved, pr-merged, agent-needs-me, agent-finished)
      --recipient <who>       add: who is told (one of: me, reviewer, channel) (default: the first the event allows)
      --channel <name>        add, with --recipient channel: one of the connection’s channels
      --repos <a,b>           add: repository names, comma separated (default: every repository that uses the connection)
      --template <text>       add: the message text (default: the event’s default message)
      --mode <mode>           add: ask before sending, or send (auto is kept only for messages to yourself, or after `consent`) (one of: ask, auto) (default: ask)
      --away-only             add, agent events: only while you are away from this Mac
      --disabled              add: save it switched off

Common options:
      --json                  Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet                 Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes                   Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help                  Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman slack rules
  foreman slack rules add --event pr-ready --recipient channel --channel eng-reviews --repos api
  foreman slack rules consent 3fa91c2b

Exit codes:
  1  You answered no, so nothing changed
  6  Needs confirmation: run it in a terminal or add --yes
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Rules decide which GitHub and agent events send a Slack message and to whom. Messages to other people ask first
in the app unless the rule has your consent; `consent` prints exactly what would go out, and to whom, and asks.
The consent covers the rule as it is: changing any part of it asks again.
```

### foreman git-backup

```text
Back up and restore your configuration through a Git repository

Usage:
  foreman git-backup [status|configure <remote>|create-repo <name>|now|preview <remote>|restore <remote>] [options]

Arguments:
  <verb>                  status (the default), configure, create-repo, now, preview or restore (one of: status, configure, create-repo, now, preview, restore) (optional)
  <target>                configure, preview, restore: the remote (a Git URL); create-repo: the new repository’s name (optional)

Options:
      --account <login>   A signed-in `gh` account, for github.com remotes
      --daily             configure: back up once a day while Foreman is open
      --no-daily          configure: stop the daily backup
      --categories <a,b>  restore: settings, templates, repos, workspaces (default: all four)

Common options:
      --json              Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet             Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes               Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help              Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman git-backup
  foreman git-backup create-repo foreman-backup
  foreman git-backup configure git@github.com:me/foreman-backup.git --daily
  foreman git-backup restore git@github.com:me/foreman-backup.git --categories settings,templates

Exit codes:
  1  You answered no, so nothing changed
  6  Needs confirmation: run it in a terminal or add --yes
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Git backup keeps your settings, templates, repository list and workspaces in a Git repository you choose, so another
computer can restore them. It never includes secrets: a restore lists the environment variables to set again.

  status                          Whether it is set up, the last backup and the last error
  configure <remote> [--account a] [--daily|--no-daily]
                                  Choose the remote (a Git URL; the user name and password never print) and whether it
                                  backs up once a day while Foreman is open
  create-repo <name> [--account a]
                                  Create a private GitHub repository and set it up
  now                             Push a backup now
  preview <remote>                What restoring would change here, without changing anything
  restore <remote> [--categories settings,templates,repos,workspaces]
                                  Shows the preview, asks, then restores exactly that preview

Restoring overwrites the settings and templates you pick on this computer, so it asks and is refused from inside an agent turn.
```

```text
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
```


### foreman cloud status

```text
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman cloud status
  foreman cloud status api-fix --json

Each remote workspace’s provider, sandbox state (running, sleeping, capped, …), size, how long it has been idle against how long the repository lets it idle before it sleeps, and whether a turn was left running while Foreman was disconnected (`foreman cloud reattach`).
```

### foreman cloud continue

```text
Continue a chat the sandbox’s session limit cut off

Usage:
  foreman cloud continue <workspace> [--tab n]

Arguments:
  <workspace>    A name, id or branch from `foreman status`, or "." for the one you’re in

Options:
  -t, --tab <n>  Open tab to use, counting from 1 (default: the only open tab)

Common options:
      --json     Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet    Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes      Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help     Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman cloud continue api-fix --tab 1

Exit codes:
  0  Done (with --wait: the turn completed)
  1  Failed, or with --wait the turn failed, was stopped or was interrupted
  2  Usage error, or --wait timed out (the turn keeps running)
  5  The connection to Foreman was lost (the turn is unaffected)
  7  Refused: an agent turn needs the repository’s “Let agents start workspaces and queue messages”
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Wakes the sandbox and sends the chat a message to carry on from where the limit stopped it; it prints the turn id.

This puts a message in a chat tab, the same one the Git panel's button sends, and queues it behind a
turn that is already running. It prints the turn id and the tab; with --wait it then blocks for
that turn, with the exit codes of `foreman run`. A workspace with several open tabs needs --tab
(the command lists them). From inside an agent turn it needs the repository's “Let agents start
workspaces and queue messages”.
```

```text
Per connected provider: sandboxes running against the plan’s limit, active CPU time and stops this month, and how long a session may last.
```

### foreman cloud build

```text
Build a repository’s base sandbox for remote workspaces

Usage:
  foreman cloud build [<repo>] [--wait]

Arguments:
  <repo>       A repository’s name, id or folder (optional)

Options:
      --wait   Follow the build’s output and end when it does (up to 30 minutes)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman cloud build api
  foreman cloud build api --wait

Exit codes:
  0  Started (with --wait: built)
  1  The build failed, --wait gave up, or the provider keeps no base to build (code not-supported)
  2  Usage error
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

A repository's remote workspaces can start from a base: a sandbox with the repository cloned and its install script run once.
foreman cloud build makes (or remakes) it. The build runs in the app; with --wait this command follows its output as progress
lines and ends when it does (exit 0 built, exit 1 failed, up to 30 minutes). Providers that keep no base (E2B) refuse (JSON code
not-supported, exit 1) and nothing is started.
```

### foreman cloud preflight

```text
Say whether a remote workspace can be made in a repository now, and why not

Usage:
  foreman cloud preflight [<repo>]

Arguments:
  <repo>       A repository’s name, id or folder (optional)

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations
  -h, --help   Show this command’s help

Examples:
  foreman cloud preflight
  foreman cloud preflight api --json

Exit codes:
  0  One can be made
  1  One can’t be made now (the reason is printed)
  Every code: foreman help exit-codes

Checks what the New workspace dialog checks before offering Remote: the feature is on, the provider is connected, the repository has a base where the provider keeps one, and the limit isn’t reached.
```

### foreman attention

```text
List what needed your attention lately, or mark it seen

Common options:
      --json   Print the result as JSON (FOREMAN_JSON=1 does the same)
  -q, --quiet  Hide progress lines and notes
  -y, --yes    Answer yes to confirmations

  foreman attention
  foreman attention --words
  foreman attention seen

Home’s Recent history: turns that finished or stopped, approvals asked and answered, CI failures, merged pull requests and agents’ reports, newest first, repeats folded into one line with a count. `seen` is “Mark all seen”: it moves only the history’s marker and resolves nothing. --words says each line as a sentence (“2 minutes ago: Claude Code finished in api-fix.”; a request still waiting says what it is), for a screen reader; with --json it changes nothing.
```
